claims.text: NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory high-entropy or multi-principal-element alloy.
The as-cast or minimally processed NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 baseline has a relatively low dislocation density.
Controlled cold rolling followed by tailored annealing can systematically increase or vary the dislocation density in NbTaHfTiZrV0.5.
Dislocation density and its spatial distribution are governing structural mediators of the alloy's deformation behavior.
Plastic deformation of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 at elevated temperatures is controlled by dislocation slip rather than deformation twinning.
A higher pre-existing dislocation density promotes more active dislocation slip and stronger dislocation interactions.
Dislocation interactions modify work-hardening behavior in this alloy.
Dislocation interactions alter internal stress fields and thereby modify thermoelastic recovery during deformation.
Increasing dislocation density will raise the high-temperature yield strength relative to an as-cast baseline.
Increasing dislocation density will alter, and likely increase, the apparent high-temperature thermoelastic modulus relative to an as-cast baseline.
The relevant tensile-test temperature range is 673–873 K.
Testing cold-worked and annealed specimens against as-cast specimens at identical strain rates provides the proposed controlled comparison.
Grain size and texture must be held approximately constant or measured to isolate the effect of dislocation density.
Cold rolling and annealing may introduce microstructural changes other than dislocation-density changes, including grain refinement or texture changes.
TEM and EBSD can be used to quantify dislocation density for the proposed comparison.
The apparent thermoelastic modulus can be derived from early-stage strain recovery in the stress-strain response.
The hypothesis is falsified if specimens with verified higher dislocation density show neither statistically higher yield strength nor altered thermoelastic behavior relative to as-cast controls.
